paragraphs.heading: What a salt marsh is
paragraphs.text: A salt marsh is a tidal wetland high on the shore between land and sea, flooded again and again by tides of seawater or brackish water. It is also called a saltmarsh, a salting or a coastal marsh. Dense stands of salt-tolerant herbs, grasses and low shrubs cover it. These plants came originally from the land, and they hold the marsh together by trapping and binding sediment.

paragraphs.heading: Where they form
paragraphs.text: Salt marshes grow on calm, low-energy shores in temperate and high latitudes. These shores are usually mud or sand flats, also called tidal flats, fed with sediment carried in by rivers and streams. Typical sites are sheltered ones, such as estuaries, embankments and the sheltered side of barrier islands and spits. A marsh shore can be stable, emerging or submerging, depending on how sediment buildup compares with the relative rise in sea level. In the tropics and subtropics mangroves take their place, with salt-tolerant trees instead of herbaceous plants.

paragraphs.heading: How a marsh builds itself
paragraphs.text: A marsh begins when a tidal flat gains height as sediment piles up, so the tide covers it for less time and plants can settle. Rivers slow down as they meet the gentle slope of the flat, and the rising tide holds the water back, so mud drops out. Mats of blue-green algae catch fine silt and clay on their sticky sheaths and make it harder to wash away. Pioneer plants such as Salicornia then trap more mud around their stems and leaves, building low mounds that join into terraces bound from below by roots. As the surface rises, tides cover it less deeply and less often, so plants that prefer higher ground move in and a series of plant communities follows.

paragraphs.heading: Life in the marsh
paragraphs.text: Salt marshes hold complex food webs. At the base are producers such as vascular plants, macroalgae, diatoms and phytoplankton, then first-level consumers such as zooplankton, molluscs and insects, and then the animals that eat those. The calm water and tall grasses give animals a refuge. Many sea fish use marshes as nurseries for their young before moving to open water, and birds may raise chicks among the grasses, safe from predators and close to food such as trapped fish, insects, shellfish and worms. Marshes also carry nutrients to coastal waters and help protect the coast.

paragraphs.heading: Kinds and places
paragraphs.text: Salt marshes take different forms depending on their setting, including delta, estuary, back-barrier, open-coast, bay and drowned-valley marshes. Delta marshes sit beside big rivers, such as the Rhône delta in France, the Ebro delta in Spain and the Mississippi River Delta in the United States. Back-barrier marshes, formed on the landward side of barriers, are common along the eastern US coast and the Frisian Islands of the Wadden Sea. The Wadden Sea alone holds nearly 40,000 hectares of salt marsh, about a fifth of Europe's coastal total. Large shallow bays hold them too, for example Britain's Morecambe Bay and North America's Bay of Fundy.

paragraphs.heading: Threats and recovery
paragraphs.text: Salt marshes have long suffered from poor coastal management, with land reclaimed for human use and pollution from farming and industry upstream. Rising seas caused by climate change now threaten other marshes by eroding and drowning them. Since the 1980s, though, wider recognition of their value for wildlife, productivity and services such as storing carbon has brought more restoration and care. One cautious estimate puts the world's saltmarsh area at about 90,800 km². The largest marshes lie outside the tropics, notably along the low-lying, ice-free shores of the North Atlantic.
